citation: Granger et al. (2025), Journal of Clinical Medicine
title: Pain Neuroscience Education on Reducing Opioid Dependency in African American and Caucasian Populations: A Narrative Review
authors: Austin Granger; Ersilia Mirabelli; Masahiro Kohzuki
pain_condition_detail: chronic pain conditions including chronic low back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with focus on nociplastic pain
context_note: US-focused review on African American and Caucasian populations in the context of the opioid epidemic.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an explanatory framework and intervention rationale, linking biological (neuroplasticity, nociplastic pain), psychological (pain catastrophizing, self-efficacy, fear), and social (ethnic disparities, healthcare access, trust) factors in a narrative synthesis, but without formal integration or testing of mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes that maladaptive neuroplasticity (biological) and ethnic disparities in prescribing access and pain beliefs (psychosocial) intersect to influence opioid use, but no specific pathway or mediator is detailed for the triadic claim.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper asserts a triadic BPS framework but does not specify mechanisms linking biological, psychological, and social domains beyond co-occurrence
conceptual_tensions_2: The term 'faulty pain cognitions' is used broadly without clear definition or operationalization
conceptual_tensions_3: Social support is identified as important but the paper notes a lack of research on its role in OUD treatment outcomes
additional_observations_1: The paper uniquely integrates general systems theory and ecological systems theory as meta-frameworks for the BPS model
additional_observations_2: The review is a narrative synthesis without systematic search or quality appraisal, limiting its evidentiary weight
additional_observations_3: The paper calls for future research incorporating readiness-to-change models and neuroimaging to study ethnic differences in PNE response
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses BPS as an organizing framework to link neuroplasticity, psychological factors, and ethnic disparities in opioid use, but integration remains descriptive rather than mechanistic. The paper is notable for its explicit use of systems theories and its focus on ethnocultural factors, but lacks formal definition of key psychological constructs and does not specify cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Typology is multifactorial because all three domains are substantively present but treated in parallel without mechanistic integration. Triadic integration is descriptive: the paper asserts intersection but no pathway. Close call on social domain: elaborated due to detailed discussion of ethnic disparities, healthcare access, and trust.

citation: Granger et al. (2025), Journal of Clinical Medicine
title: Pain Neuroscience Education on Reducing Opioid Dependency in African American and Caucasian Populations: A Narrative Review
authors: Austin Granger; Ersilia Mirabelli; Masahiro Kohzuki
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain with nociplastic mechanisms and opioid use disorder in African American and Caucasian patients in a physical therapy setting.
context_note: American focus on African American and Caucasian populations; disparities in prescribing, access, provider bias, trust, socioeconomic status, and cultural pain beliefs.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS by using systems/ecological theory to organize a narrative review of nociplastic pain mechanisms, opioid prescribing disparities, pain beliefs, and PNE. PNE is framed as a biopsychosocial intervention that changes faulty pain cognitions, stress/fear/anxiety, and trust-related processing to reduce opioid dependence; no variables are tested as a formal BPS model.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposed pathways are narrative: PNE changes faulty pain cognitions and stress/fear/anxiety, which may calm central processing and reduce pain and opioid use; pain beliefs, provider trust, and ethnic disparities modulate pain processing and opioid prescribing/access. No tested causal model is reported.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS to critique biomedical reductionism, yet its evidence base is narrative and cannot make causal claims
conceptual_tensions_2: Ethnic disparities are used as explanatory factors, but the paper cautions that individual pain responses remain unique
conceptual_tensions_3: PNE is framed as promising for reducing opioid dependence, but no statistical analysis or experimental design is included
conceptual_tensions_4: Provider trust and provider ethnicity are proposed as modulators of pain brain activity, but the review reports this as future research
conceptual_tensions_5: Social support is treated as important, yet studies disagree and qualitative perspectives are called for
additional_observations_1: The review includes quantitative, qualitative, and other review articles in its methods
additional_observations_2: Search terms cover central sensitization, peripheral processing mechanisms, central processing mechanisms, ion channel expression, pain neuromatrix, and graded motor imagery
additional_observations_3: PNE is consistently framed as adjunctive to physical therapy, especially active movement, GMI, manual therapy, or exercise therapy
additional_observations_4: OUD is treated as a chronic disorder with physical, social, and mental health implications rather than only a substance-use outcome
additional_observations_5: Buprenorphine is discussed as affecting depression, anxiety, stress, and quality of life in OUD recovery
additional_observations_6: The paper calls for fMRI studies comparing PNE and GMI across ethnicities
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a systems/ecological rationale for PNE in chronic pain and OUD. It links nociplastic mechanisms, pain beliefs, provider trust, prescribing disparities, and social support, but the integration is narrative and largely cross-domain association rather than tested causal modelling.
coding_rationale: True integrative because all three domains are linked through PNE, pain beliefs, disparities, and neuroplasticity; no formal BPS model is tested.

title: Pain Neuroscience Education on Reducing Opioid Dependency in African American and Caucasian Populations: A Narrative Review
authors: Austin Granger; Ersilia Mirabelli; Masahiro Kohzuki
pain_condition_detail: opioid dependence and chronic pain in African American and Caucasian populations
context_note: United States, focusing on racial/ethnic disparities in pain management and opioid prescribing
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS as an explanatory framework for understanding how PNE reduces opioid dependency through addressing biological (neuroplasticity), psychological (pain cognitions), and social (ethnic disparities) factors, but does not specify mechanisms of integration between domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and lack of specified integration mechanisms between domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Gap between neuroimaging evidence of ethnic differences and lack of experimental PNE studies across ethnicities
conceptual_tensions_3: Discrepancy between described importance of social factors and their limited operationalization in treatment recommendations
additional_observations_1: The review positions PNE as an intervention grounded in BPS principles but does not demonstrate how the three domains are integrated in practice
additional_observations_2: Ethnic disparities are discussed primarily through social and cultural lenses, with biological mechanisms (frontostriatal activity) presented as correlates rather than integrated pathways
additional_observations_3: The review identifies readiness-to-change models as needed for PNE implementation but does not operationalize them within the BPS framework
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the biopsychosocial model as an explanatory framework for understanding how pain neuroscience education reduces opioid dependency, with elaborated coverage of biological (neuroplasticity, pain neuromatrix), psychological (pain catastrophizing, self-efficacy), and social (ethnic disparities, provider bias) factors. However, it does not specify mechanisms of integration between these domains, representing a multifactorial rather than integrative BPS approach. The review identifies key gaps in ethnic-specific PNE research and calls for experimental designs incorporating readiness-to-change models.
coding_rationale: BPS typology as multifactorial due to elaborated domain coverage without specified integration mechanisms. Triadic integration scored as 'none' because no cross-domain pathways are specified despite all three domains being present.
